auditor: Center for New York City Affairs
title: Dignified Pay for Quality Care: What New York’s Family Child Care Providers Need to Thrive
plain_title: What New York City's home-based child care providers earn
what_they_audited: A report from the Center for New York City Affairs at The New School on the finances and working conditions of licensed home-based child care providers in New York City. It draws on a survey of 465 family child care (FCC) and group family child care (GFCC) providers and follow-up focus groups with 59 of them.
background: Family child care and group family child care providers are small business owners and independent contractors who look after children in their own homes, and they are part of the city's publicly subsidized early care and education (ECE) system. Since Pre-K launched in 2014 the city has lost 1,400 of these businesses.

findings.plain: Counting only the hours their programs are open, the median family child care provider earned $7.33 an hour in 2023 and the median group family child care provider earned $5.98. The minimum wage that year was $15.
Almost half of family child care providers and a quarter of group providers do not pay themselves a set wage at all. What they take home is whatever is left after business expenses are covered.

findings.plain: City contracts pay home-based programs far less than centers for the same service. The extended-day contract for network-affiliated home providers pays $16,900 per child per year, against the $27,473 the city paid the average center-based program in fiscal year 2025.

recommendations: Set public voucher and contract rates using a true cost of care method that reflects what it actually costs to run an early care and education program, including paying staff and providers.

Move to universal child care in New York so all families, regardless of income or immigration status, can get subsidized care with no or low-cost co-pays, with every seat paid through public vouchers or contracts.
Build a sector-wide career ladder that guarantees comparable pay for comparable work across all program types.
Run a public marketing campaign covering all early care and education programs that explains that 3-K and Pre-K are part of a broader sector and describes what home-based programs offer.
Create a state or city wage subsidy fund to close the gap between current pay and a minimum wage standard for each early care and education occupation.
Replace or improve city websites such as MyCity.nyc.gov with one that holds all information on child care supply and options, searchable and mapped, and linked to applications for subsidized care.
Develop a new marketing campaign that educates the public about all early care and education programs at once and about how families can afford them.
Commit city revenue to keep existing subsidized options open to all eligible families even when federal Child Care and Block Grant funds fall short.
Submit an annual report to the City Council evaluating capacity and utilization across private and public early care and education programs.
Work with the Fund for the City of New York to amend its Returnable Grant Fund rules so home-based providers can get interest-free loans when city agencies pay late.
Hold an annual City Council hearing with every agency involved in the early care and education system, along with community organizations, networks, providers and parents.
Amend city law, alongside state legislation, to include family child care and group family child care providers in existing public pension programs.
Overhaul or replace the Administration for Children's Services Childcare Attendance & Payment System so providers can log enrollment and attendance and be paid accurately and on time.
Implement presumptive eligibility so the city can cover the cost of care while the Administration for Children's Services determines whether a family qualifies for a voucher.

Have the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene tell providers expected processing times for licenses and staff background checks and who to contact, and work with the state to speed those checks up.
Have the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene work with the state to write a plain-language policy, in multiple languages, for site visits, violations and grievances.
Run an inspection process that balances technical assistance and public safety, pairing providers with the same inspectors where that makes sense.
Have the Human Resources Administration partner with community organizations to help providers keep Medicaid, food benefits and other assistance.
Have New York City Public Schools use a true cost of care method in its next five-year contract with family child care networks for programs such as 3-K.
Have New York City Public Schools work with networks and providers so providers can engage with parents during the 3-K enrollment process.
